system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 7: Giant Lines – Going Deeper into the Flux & Reflux over D7(9)

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 7 — Giant Lines – Going Deeper into the Flux & Reflux over D7(9)

_Pages 27-37._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Extended scale options: guide chords required

> In the following examples we have some extended scale options that can also work very well.
> Notice that in these cases we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what
> we are doing.

**Significance (p. 27).** This establishes the core rule that extended scale lines require a minimum of two guide chords for proper fretboard visualization, which is the foundational constraint governing all three ideas that follow.

## Melodic minor: no avoid notes

> the melodic minor scale has no avoid notes, and for that reason we
>     can have a bigger variety of scale arpeggios and guide chords.

**Significance (p. 28).** This defines the key theoretical property of the melodic minor scale that justifies the expanded set of scale arpeggio options presented throughout the chapter.

## Melodic minor chord family

> The next scale arpeggios can be applyed over any chord derived from "A" melodic minor
>     scale: Am(maj7) or Am6, Bsus(b9), Cmaj7(#5), *D7(9, #11, 13), *E7(9, b13), F#ø, G#7alt.

**Significance (p. 28).** This lists all seven diatonic chords of the A melodic minor scale that the subsequent scale arpeggios apply to, anchoring every fingering example that follows to a specific harmonic context.

## D7(#11) dual function warning

> D7(#11) is the IV degre from the "A" melodic minor scale
>     chord family. However, this chord also can be considered as a dominant diminished chord
>     voicing possibility. Maybe you are asking yourself: So what? As a matter of a fact, we must
>     know that in some cases we cannot use certain types of scales and chords, otherwise we
>     might have a terrible result.

**Significance (p. 28).** This is a critical rule-of-avoidance: it warns the player that a chord's dual identity (melodic minor IV vs. dominant diminished voicing) constrains which scales and chords can safely be used over it.

## Melodic minor tensions: not all required

> * The chords { D7(9,#11, 13), E7(9, b13) } do not have to contain all the tensions presented.
>     However, we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing
>     or improvising.

**Significance (p. 28).** This rule clarifies the difference between voicing practice and theoretical knowledge: not every tension need be voiced, but all must be known to avoid harmonization and improvisation errors.

## Cm key: visualizing Eb substitution

> In order to not start doing a big mess with all these options, we will learn this new scale
> arpeggios in the key of "Cm" thus helping us to visualize the "Eb" note replacing "E" note.
> Remember that the secret is to relate the melodic idea with the chord shape given.

**Significance (p. 30).** This gives a concrete pedagogical method — using Cm as the reference key — and states the method's organizing principle: every melodic idea must be visualized in relation to its associated chord shape.

## Visualizing melodic minor tetrads per zone

> In order to better visualize the melodic minor tetrads on the guitar fretboard, let’s use the
> guiding chords we have learned before: Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7). All the tetrads from the
> melodic minor family should be related to these two chords.

**Significance (p. 33).** This establishes the two master guide chords — Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7) — as the universal reference shapes for locating every melodic minor tetrad across all fretboard zones.

CHAPTER FILE>>>
